questions.stem: A single radar range to a charted lighthouse puts the ship on what?
options: A straight line through the lighthouse
A circle of position centred on the lighthouse
A fixed point
A line parallel to the coast
questions.explanation: Distance alone does not give direction. The ship could be anywhere on the circle whose radius is the range. A second range gives a second circle and a fix.

questions.stem: Why is a fix from two radar ranges preferred to range and bearing of one object?
options: Radar bearing is always exact
Ranges can be measured on the longitude scale
Two ranges need no identification of the objects
Radar range is more accurate than radar bearing
questions.explanation: Range depends on the timing of the echo; bearing depends on beam width and the heading reference, so it is the weaker measurement.

questions.stem: Two range arcs cross at two points about 6 nm apart. The DR is within 1 nm of one of them. What do you do?
options: Take the crossing farthest from the DR
Take the midpoint of the two
Take the crossing nearest the DR, and confirm with a bearing or third range if in doubt
Reject both and use the DR
questions.explanation: Two circles intersect at two points. The DR picks the right one; a third line removes the doubt.

questions.stem: At what angle should two range arcs ideally cross as seen from the ship?
options: About 10 degrees
About 90 degrees
About 180 degrees
About 0 degrees
questions.explanation: The best crossing is at right angles. Objects nearly in line produce nearly tangent circles and a poor fix.

questions.stem: A lighthouse at 49 degrees 00.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 30.0 minutes W is 2.4 nm away on a bearing of 090 degrees true from the ship. cos 49 degrees = 0.656. What is the ship's position?
options: 49 degrees 00.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 26.3 minutes W
49 degrees 02.4 minutes N, 123 degrees 30.0 minutes W
49 degrees 00.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 32.4 minutes W
49 degrees 00.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 33.7 minutes W
questions.explanation: The ship is on the reciprocal, 270 degrees, from the lighthouse. Departure 2.4 nm west; difference of longitude = 2.4 / 0.656 = 3.7 minutes W, so 123 degrees 33.7 minutes W. East of the light (26.3) is the wrong side, and 32.4 forgets to divide by the cosine.

questions.stem: The echo sounder reads 9.6 m below the transducer, which is 0.6 m below the waterline. The height of tide is 2.2 m. What depth do you compare with the chart?
questions.explanation: Depth of water = 9.6 + 0.6 = 10.2 m. Charted equivalent = depth of water - height of tide = 10.2 - 2.2 = 8.0 m. 6.8 subtracts the transducer offset, 12.4 adds the tide, and 7.4 omits the offset.

questions.stem: A single echo-sounder reading matches a charted sounding. What does that tell you?
options: It is a fix, because depth is unique
It proves the chart is out of date
It replaces the need for a DR
It is consistent with your position but not a fix, because many places have the same depth
questions.explanation: A depth is a check. A well-defined contour can act as a line of position, but one sounding alone is not a fix.

questions.stem: Where is a radar range measured with dividers read off the chart?
options: On the latitude scale at the side of the chart, level with the work
On the longitude scale along the bottom
On the scale in the title block
On the compass rose
questions.explanation: The length of a minute of latitude changes with latitude on a Mercator chart, so use the part of the side scale level with the work.

questions.stem: Which radar target is best for a range fix?
options: A low sloping beach with no distinct edge
A steep-to cliff or small islet that is clearly identified on the display and the chart
An unidentified echo
A large area of rain clutter
questions.explanation: Choose well-defined, positively identified objects. Low shores return echoes from somewhere inland of the charted waterline.

questions.stem: Radar gives you the range and the bearing of one lighthouse at the same instant. What can you say about the resulting position?
options: It is a fix, but a weaker one than two ranges because it carries the bearing error
It is exact because both measurements come from the same object
It is only an estimated position, never a fix
It needs a third object to be a fix
questions.explanation: The range and bearing of one object give a fix, but the bearing error is carried into it, which is why two ranges are preferred.
